p: The battle opened here. On the morning of July 1, 1863, Confederate infantry under Henry Heth pushed east along the Chambersburg Pike toward the town of Gettysburg, expecting little resistance. Instead they ran into dismounted Union cavalry under John Buford, who fought a stubborn delaying action across these ridges to buy time for the infantry marching up behind him.

p.short: Site tour stop 1, McPherson Ridge, paragraph 1 of 3

p: The Union First Corps arrived under Major General John Reynolds, who rushed his men into the fight near McPherson's Woods. He was killed almost immediately — one of the highest-ranking officers to die in the entire battle. The hard-fighting Iron Brigade held this ground through brutal close-range combat.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 1, McPherson Ridge, paragraph 2 of 3

p: By late afternoon, overwhelming Confederate numbers pressing from the west and north finally cracked the Union line. The defenders fell back through the streets of Gettysburg to the high ground at Cemetery Hill — setting the stage for two more days of fighting. The McPherson barn still stands near here as a landmark of where it all began.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 1, McPherson Ridge, paragraph 3 of 3

p: An exposed salient. General Dan Sickles posted his Union corps in and around this orchard, thrusting his line far out ahead of the army to seize slightly higher ground. It left his men dangerously exposed on two sides at once.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 10, The Peach Orchard, paragraph 1 of 3

p: For a while, Federal cannon here hammered the advancing Confederates as they crossed the Rose Farm. But around 6:30 p.m., Longstreet's assault smashed into the salient from the front and the flank together, and the position gave way.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 10, The Peach Orchard, paragraph 2 of 3

p: The breaking of the Peach Orchard sent Union troops streaming back toward Cemetery Ridge and nearly tore open the center of Meade's line — a crisis contained only barely, and only as darkness fell.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 10, The Peach Orchard, paragraph 3 of 3

p: The Bloody Run. This low, marshy stream lies in the hollow between the Peach Orchard and Cemetery Ridge. As the Union line to the south gave way, shattered regiments fell back across this ground under heavy fire.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 11, Plum Run, paragraph 1 of 3

p: So many wounded men dragged themselves to its banks for water that the creek earned a grim nickname — the “Bloody Run.” The fighting here was confused and desperate, waged in failing light among the boulders and brush.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 11, Plum Run, paragraph 2 of 3

p: It was here that small bands of Union reinforcements bought precious minutes with their lives, slowing the Confederate advance just long enough for the threatened center to be shored up.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 11, Plum Run, paragraph 3 of 3

p: Holding the center. The largest monument on the entire battlefield rises here, honoring the more than 34,000 Pennsylvania soldiers who fought the battle on their home state's soil. Bronze tablets around its base record their names.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 12, Pennsylvania Memorial, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Late on July 2, this stretch of Cemetery Ridge was held by little more than Union artillery as the Confederate attacks to the south threatened to break clean through. Meade hurried infantry over from other parts of the line to fill the gap.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 12, Pennsylvania Memorial, paragraph 2 of 3

p: The line held. By keeping its grip on the center here, the Union army denied Lee the breakthrough he sought — and set the stage for his even greater gamble the next day.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 12, Pennsylvania Memorial, paragraph 3 of 3

p: The fight for Culp's Hill. On the Union far right, the battle took a different shape among the wooded heights of Culp's Hill. Around 7 p.m. on July 2, Confederates seized the lower slopes here while many of the hill's defenders had been pulled away to help elsewhere.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 13, Spangler's Spring, paragraph 1 of 3

p: Through the night both sides dug in among the rocks and trees, sometimes only yards apart. At dawn on July 3 a thunderous seven-hour battle erupted to drive the Confederates back off the hill.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 13, Spangler's Spring, paragraph 2 of 3

p: The cool waters of Spangler's Spring, legend holds, were shared by weary soldiers of both armies during the lulls — a small, human moment amid the slaughter.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (battlefield tour)
p.short: Site tour stop 13, Spangler's Spring, paragraph 3 of 3

p: A struggle at dusk. As night closed in on July 2, Confederate troops launched a sudden assault up the steep eastern face of Cemetery Hill, aimed straight at the heart of the Union position.
